newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala may turn to OAS after China's U.N. snub.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala may turn to OAS after China's U.N. snub.

text.p: Guatemala said on Saturday it likely would seek observers from the Organization of American States (OAS) after China vetoed a United Nations peace-keeping mission for this Central American country.

Angered over Guatemala's warm ties with Taiwan, China used its veto power late on Friday in the U.N. Security Council for the first time in nearly 24 years, frustrating Guatemala's efforts to bring in 155 unarmed U.N. peace-keepers to oversee a rebel disarmament.
The remaining 14 members of the Security Council approved the mission to help disarm 3,000 rebel fighters.
"This is really deplorable and of course represents a complication for the Guatemalan peace process," Guatemalan Foreign Minister Eduardo Stein told Reuters in a telephone interview.

The diplomatic spat has been the only hitch so far in the peace process since the Guatemalan government and leftist guerrillas of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) signed a peace treaty on Dec. 29, ending 36 years of civil war.
Stein said the country most likely would ask the OAS for help but has held out the possibility of renewing the request for peace-keepers before the U.N. General Assembly.
"I talked to (OAS Secretary General Cesar) Gaviria yesterday evening and he will send on Monday one or two high-level experts to examine details of the operation with us," Stein said.

In Beijing, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang accused Guatemala of forcing China to exercise its veto because the Central American country had maintained ties with Taiwan, which Beijing regards as a renegade province not entitled to international diplomatic links.
"We had no choice but to vote against the draft decision on peacekeeping," the Xinhua news agency quoted Shen as saying.

"Clearly, the government of Guatemala must be wholly responsible," he said and made clear that China had no objection to the dispatch of U.N. peacekeepers to oversee a peace that ended a brutal 36-year-old civil war.

Guatemala made no promises to modify relations with Taiwan, one of the five biggest foreign investors in this country. The foreign minister of Taiwan, a major supplier of foreign aid to Guatemala, was invited to the Dec. 29 peace-signing ceremony, a gesture that annoyed Beijing.
Any move that bestows recognition of Taiwan as indepedent from China angers the Communist government in Beijing.

Taiwan has targeted several other poor Central American countries for aid and investment. Those countries, in turn, have been firm backers of moves aimed at securing United Nations membership for Taiwan.

David Stephens, director of the United Nations Mission for the Verification of Human Rights in Guatemala (MINUGUA), said the delay in observers for the cease-fire and disarmament was unfortunate and would hold up the demobilization.
"This will inevitably have serious repercussions on the demobilization process because without a mandate this mission cannot make arrangements," Stephens said.
Stephens said the so-called "blue berets" -- unarmed military observers -- would have been attached to MINUGUA.
More than 100,000 people died in Guatemala's conflict, the last in Central America, and a further 40,000 "disappeared."

Under the peace accord, Guatemala's army would redeploy units to specified locations, after which troops from the rebel Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) would move to eight assembly points and disarm. The U.N. observers were to verify the process.
